Who Heard the Alarm?

Module 8 · ARDL, information, and exogeneity

Gary Cornwall

Econ 6376 · The George Washington University

Act I · Letting another variable into the room

One series’ memory becomes a relationship across series.

The selected hook is The Office’s fire drill: many people react to the same event. Our recurring visual links that common news to multiple responses. The class works without playing a clip or knowing the television show. Six acts: 15 + 30 + 25 + 25 + 30 + 10 minutes; a ten-minute break after Act III brings the planned session to 145 minutes. Adjust pacing to discussion. Canonical source: notes/module_08_notes.qmd, Core §§8.1–8.7. The last act contains only the explicitly requested optional previews (§§8.8–8.10).

ARMA: one series remembers outcomes and surprises

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+θ1ϵt−1+ϵty_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\theta_1\epsilon_{t-1}+\epsilon_t

A time-unrolled DAG: each date is a different node. Innovations ε are unobserved DGP quantities.

[3 minutes. Sources: notes §8.1, ARMA diagram; Modules 1 and 3.] Begin with the picture, not a list of learning objectives. Trace both routes from last period’s innovation into today’s outcome. Deterministic terms omitted from the graph. A DAG has no directed cycle; unrolling time allows feedback across dates. Arrows depict posited model dependencies, not evidence of causal identification.

ARDL: another series brings its own history

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵty_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t

Observed x replaces the explicit MA block. Drawing an arrow does not identify a causal effect.

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.1.] ARDL or ADL: autoregressive distributed lag. The outcome equation uses x; the dashed path is context, not a fitted second equation. The new regressors are observed variables, not past innovations. Ask: if current x is not yet released, which term can we remove? If y has no memory, which arrow disappears?

Where we are: expand the mixing board

yt=α+δt+∑j=1pϕjyt−j+∑ℓ=1qθℓϵt−ℓ+ϵty_t=\alpha+\delta t+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_jy_{t-j} +\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\theta_\ell\epsilon_{t-\ell}+\epsilon_t

Channel Module 8 baseline
Intercept and outcome memory On: α\alpha, ϕjyt−j\phi_jy_{t-j}
Trend and explicit MA memory Off
Observed predictor history New: ∑ℓ=0qβℓxt−ℓ\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell x_{t-\ell}
Current disturbance Still present; its relation to xx now matters
Module 7 combined forecasts. Today we add information absent from that forecast pool.

[2 minutes. Sources: notes §8.1; Module 7 closing handoff.] The old master equation must expand: no combination of univariate forecasts can manufacture information absent from all members. Initial claims versus unemployment will supply the real-data bridge. The q in the old master equation is MA order; the q in the new predictor block is maximum predictor lag. Next slide defines it.

One conditional equation, many possible lags

yt=α+∑j=1pϕjyt−j+∑ℓ=0qβℓxt−ℓ+ϵty_t=\alpha+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_jy_{t-j} +\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell x_{t-\ell}+\epsilon_t

Restriction Model left on the board
All βℓ=0\beta_\ell=0 AR(p)(p)
All ϕj=0\phi_j=0 Distributed-lag regression
q=0q=0 Outcome lags and current xx
β0=0\beta_0=0 Lag-only predictor block
What does ARDL(1,2) include that ARDL(1,1) does not?
Here q means the maximum x lag. It is not the MA order.

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.2.] Ask for the actual terms, not a definition: the additional beta2 x(t−2). One predictor keeps timing visible; the method permits several predictor blocks. The ARDL(1,1) stays our worked example throughout the module.

The DGP and our fitted equation remain different

DGP: parameters and disturbances we know only in a simulation

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵty_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t

Estimated equation: hats and an observed residual

yt=α̂+ϕ̂1yt−1+β̂0xt+β̂1xt−1+ety_t=\hat\alpha+\hat\phi_1y_{t-1}+\hat\beta_0x_t+\hat\beta_1x_{t-1}+e_t

et=yt−ŷte_t=y_t-\hat y_t

Fitted values: ŷ. Forecasts from Module 7 onward: ỹt+h∣t\tilde y_{t+h\mid t}.

[1 minute. Source: notes §8.2; notation dictionary L8.] Do not give a new numerical example here. Emphasize that residuals are fitted objects; they do not reveal the structural disturbance in observational data.

Keep the stationary baseline visible

Φ(L)=1−ϕ1L−⋯−ϕpLp\Phi(L)=1-\phi_1L-\cdots-\phi_pL^p

Stationary inputs + stable dynamics + suitable disturbances.
  • AR lag-polynomial roots lie outside the unit circle.
  • For one outcome lag: |ϕ1|<1|\phi_1|<1.
  • If xx responds to past yy, check stability of the joint system.
Trending levels need additional reasoning. Cointegration is a later route, not a blanket exemption.

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.2.] Enders’ characteristic roots inside are the reciprocal convention. No detailed root calculation on the deck. A regression with ARMA disturbances is also a different specification: the notes show the restricted ARDL produced by an AR(1) disturbance. Do not translate an xreg coefficient mechanically into this model.

Student reference — the root condition. For one outcome lag,

1−ϕ1L=0⇒L=1/ϕ1.1-\phi_1 L=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L=1/\phi_1.

For ϕ1≠0\phi_1\ne0, |L|>1|L|>1 is equivalent to |ϕ1|<1|\phi_1|<1. If ϕ1=0\phi_1=0, there is no autoregressive propagation and no finite AR root to check. This is the same condition expressed using reciprocal roots, not two competing definitions of stability.

Student reference — why AR(1) disturbances impose a restriction. Start with the alternative model in notes §8.2:

yt=α+βxt+ut,ut=ϕ1ut−1+ϵt.\begin{aligned} y_t&=\alpha+\beta x_t+u_t,\\ u_t&=\phi_1u_{t-1}+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

Here utu_t is the disturbance around the static regression, while ϵt\epsilon_t is its innovation. The preceding regression equation gives

ut−1=yt−1−α−βxt−1.u_{t-1}=y_{t-1}-\alpha-\beta x_{t-1}.

Substitute and collect terms:

yt=α+βxt+ϕ1(yt−1−α−βxt−1)+ϵt=(1−ϕ1)α+ϕ1yt−1+βxt−ϕ1βxt−1+ϵt.\begin{aligned} y_t&=\alpha+\beta x_t +\phi_1(y_{t-1}-\alpha-\beta x_{t-1})+\epsilon_t\\ &=(1-\phi_1)\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+\beta x_t-\phi_1\beta x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

Thus the resulting ARDL intercept is (1−ϕ1)α(1-\phi_1)\alpha, the current predictor coefficient is β\beta, and the lag coefficient is restricted to −ϕ1β-\phi_1\beta. The α\alpha in this calculation belongs to the original static regression; it is not equal to the resulting ARDL intercept. An unrestricted ARDL does not impose this coefficient restriction. Under stability its long-run step multiplier in this restricted case is

β−ϕ1β1−ϕ1=β.\frac{\beta-\phi_1\beta}{1-\phi_1}=\beta.

This is why a coefficient from a regression with AR disturbances should not be read as the unrestricted ARDL’s impact multiplier without checking the model.

Act II · Who else heard the news?

Exogeneity is the central question.

Use the instructor-selected Office fire-drill reference lightly: several people react together to the same event. The graphs below isolate a possible common driver; a scene also contains interactions, so it cannot identify the economic mechanism. No familiarity with a television series is required.

The Office: everyone reacts to the same emergency

If claims and unemployment rise in the same month, which story has the regression established?
Optional clip: The Office · Fire Drill (official). The diagram remains usable offline.

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.3 common current news; original teaching diagram.] Invite competing stories: layoffs affect both; claims provide timely measurement; there may be feedback; the definitions cover different populations. Neither co-movement nor an arrow settles which intervention would move the outcome. Optional instructor hook: the opening fire drill in The Office, Stress Relief, Part1 (S5E14). Official source and episode description: https://www.peacocktv.com/watch-online/tv/the-office/4902514835143843112/seasons/5/episodes/stress-relief-part-1-episode-14/194b509e-14fb-377a-ac23-c1ec8a412703 Official clip linked by Peacock’s twentieth-anniversary episode article: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gO8N3L_aERg If played, use only the short setup needed for the common-event analogy; no internet dependency is required to teach this slide. The drill is initiated by Dwight, so do not imply it is itself an exogenous real-world experiment. It is an analogy for shared news, not a proposed identification strategy.

Exogeneity asks what remains in the disturbance

Let ℱt−1\mathcal F_{t-1} contain the relevant histories of yy and xx.

E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0\boxed{E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0}

After using the modeled history and current x, no predictable mean component remains.
  • This covers all included regressors, including lagged yy.
  • With stability, moments, and adequate regressor variation, it supports large-sample OLS consistency.
  • It does not promise exact recovery in one finite sample.

[5 minutes. Source: notes §8.3.] Read the conditioning bar aloud. The regressor vector is (1, y(t−1), x(t), x(t−1)) in our ARDL(1,1). The sufficient condition implies orthogonality for that vector. Do not reduce the condition to Cov(x_t,epsilon_t)=0 alone. We have deliberately not imported exact textbook unbiasedness or t/F distributions from a strictly exogenous Gaussian regression. Formal conditions stay in the notes Technical Note.

Student reference — from the conditional mean to the OLS moments. Let zt=(1,yt−1,xt,xt−1)′z_t=(1,y_{t-1},x_t,x_{t-1})' for this ARDL(1,1). Every component is known given ℱt−1\mathcal F_{t-1} and xtx_t. Assuming the products are integrable, the law of iterated expectations gives

E[ztϵt]=E[E[ztϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]]=E[ztE[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]]=E[zt0]=0.\begin{aligned} E[z_t\epsilon_t] &=E\!\left[E[z_t\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\right]\\ &=E\!\left[z_t E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\right]\\ &=E[z_t\,0]=0. \end{aligned}

The same argument applies component by component to every included outcome lag and predictor lag. Merely showing that one covariance is zero would not prove this conditional-mean statement.

Optional technical reference — where consistency enters. Write yt=zt′ϑ+ϵty_t=z_t'\vartheta+\epsilon_t. For a nonsingular sample regressor matrix, substitute that equation into the OLS formula:

ϑ̂=(∑tztzt′)−1∑tztyt=ϑ+(∑tztzt′)−1∑tztϵt,ϑ̂−ϑ=(T−1∑tztzt′)−1(T−1∑tztϵt).\begin{aligned} \hat\vartheta &=\left(\sum_t z_tz_t'\right)^{-1}\sum_t z_ty_t\\ &=\vartheta+ \left(\sum_t z_tz_t'\right)^{-1}\sum_tz_t\epsilon_t,\\ \hat\vartheta-\vartheta &=\left(T^{-1}\sum_tz_tz_t'\right)^{-1} \left(T^{-1}\sum_tz_t\epsilon_t\right). \end{aligned}

Under stationary/ergodic sampling and suitable moments, the sample averages converge to E[ztzt′]E[z_tz_t'] and zero. If E[ztzt′]E[z_tz_t'] is positive definite, the estimation error converges to zero. This is the argument in the notes’ Technical Note; it supplies neither exact finite-sample unbiasedness nor exact t/Ft/F distributions. Inference needs its own variance and central-limit conditions.

Three claims that sound similar

x and y are relatedOften why we included x. This is not the exogeneity restriction.
ε has no serial correlationA statement about the disturbance across dates.
E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0A statement about the disturbance relative to the regressor information.
Could two white-noise shocks be correlated with each other today?
Yes. No memory is not independence from every other process.

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.3, Three Different Relationships.] Intentional fragment: solicit the prediction before revealing the answer. Students often carry the L5 white-noise diagnostic further than it can go. Today’s x innovation can reveal today’s y disturbance even when neither has memory.

Common current news creates an omitted route

If the outcome disturbance contains shared news, current x may reveal part of that disturbance.

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.3.] The original full DAG also contains lagged y and lagged x; omitted here only to focus attention on the new current route. This is a candidate mechanism. No opposing same-period arrows: that would not be a DAG. In the next act we know the mechanism because we construct it ourselves.

Lagged feedback is a different issue

xt=0.5xt−1+0.2yt−1+ϵx,tx_t=0.5x_{t-1}+0.2y_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}

With independent current shocks, independent of the past, this feedback can coexist with our conditional-mean restriction.

[5 minutes. Source: notes §8.3 and simulation §8.4.] The graph isolates an across-date route present in the model; the complete equations have other arrows too. Today’s y disturbance enters y_t, which can affect tomorrow’s x. It need not predict today’s x innovation. Sequential conditioning permits this distinction. Joint stability still matters and is checked for the simulation. Ask students to explain why ‘feedback’ alone is too vague a verdict.

Student reference — current exogeneity and future dependence can coexist. Use the feedback-only case: c=0.2c=0.2, independent current shocks, and shock pairs independent across dates. Conditional on ℱt−1\mathcal F_{t-1} and xtx_t, the outcome’s predictable component is

gt=0.2+0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1,g_t=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1},

so yt=gt+ϵty_t=g_t+\epsilon_t. Because current xtx_t depends on the past and ϵx,t\epsilon_{x,t}, it does not reveal the independent ϵt\epsilon_t:

E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0.E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]=0.

But the next predictor value is

xt+1=0.5xt+0.2yt+ϵx,t+1=0.5xt+0.2gt+0.2ϵt+ϵx,t+1.\begin{aligned} x_{t+1}&=0.5x_t+0.2y_t+\epsilon_{x,t+1}\\ &=0.5x_t+0.2g_t+0.2\epsilon_t+\epsilon_{x,t+1}. \end{aligned}

Holding the current information fixed, the two remaining shocks are independent and have unit variance. Therefore

Cov(ϵt,xt+1∣ℱt−1,xt)=0.2Var(ϵt)=0.2.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_t,x_{t+1} \mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t) &=0.2\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_t)=0.2. \end{aligned}

The route is ϵt→yt→xt+1\epsilon_t\rightarrow y_t\rightarrow x_{t+1}. The unconditional covariance is also 0.2 here: ϵt\epsilon_t is mean independent of the current information. Thus a zero conditional mean given the entire predictor path cannot hold, even though the sequential restriction does hold. The calculation depends on the independent-shock construction; it is not a universal formula for feedback.

Optional technical reference — checking joint stability. Substitute the predictor equation into the outcome equation:

yt=0.2+(0.6+0.4c)yt−1+0.4xt−1+0.4ϵx,t+ϵt,xt=cyt−1+0.5xt−1+ϵx,t.\begin{aligned} y_t&=0.2+(0.6+0.4c)y_{t-1}+0.4x_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+0.4\epsilon_{x,t}+\epsilon_t,\\ x_t&=c\,y_{t-1}+0.5x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}. \end{aligned}

For c=0.2c=0.2, the transition matrix for (yt,xt)′(y_t,x_t)' is

A=(0.680.40.20.5).A=\begin{pmatrix}0.68&0.4\\0.2&0.5\end{pmatrix}.

Its characteristic roots solve

0=(λ−0.68)(λ−0.5)−0.4(0.2)=λ2−1.18λ+0.26,λ=1.18±1.182−4(0.26)2≈0.887,0.293.\begin{aligned} 0&=(\lambda-0.68)(\lambda-0.5)-0.4(0.2)\\ &=\lambda^2-1.18\lambda+0.26,\\ \lambda&=\frac{1.18\pm\sqrt{1.18^2-4(0.26)}}{2}\\ &\approx0.887,\;0.293. \end{aligned}

Both characteristic roots are inside the unit circle, equivalently the joint lag-polynomial roots are outside. For the two no-feedback cases the transition matrix is triangular, with characteristic roots 0.6 and 0.5. Changing current shock correlation changes the innovation covariance, not these transition roots. This verifies the simulation’s stability claim; the matrix machinery is optional reference and is developed in Module 11.

Stronger assumptions and narrower diagnostics

Strict exogeneity asks today’s disturbance to be unrelated to the entire xx path—including future xx.

Lagged feedback may violate that stronger requirement while the sequential conditional mean remains valid.

Proposed fix What it cannot establish
“Use a lag” Earlier does not guarantee exogenous
“The residual ACF looks clean” No proof of structural exogeneity
“Use HAC standard errors” No repair for invalid coefficient moments
Are we making a prediction claim, a conditional-path claim, or a causal claim?

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.3.] This question is the bridge to the experiment and later application. Strict exogeneity is defined verbally at the notes’ Core depth. We need not impose it merely to state the sequential conditional equation. Robust variance estimates have a role when the coefficient estimator’s moments are valid; they cannot make a wrong target into a right one. Causal invariance requires extra reasoning.

Act III · Build it, then break it

Same structural coefficients. Different information.

The simulation is the center of gravity: build the pair of equations, change only feedback or current-shock correlation, predict, then inspect outcomes. The notes’ helpers supply reusable code; the for-loop on screen exposes the DGP.

Two equations we control

xt=0.5xt−1+cyt−1+ϵx,t,yt=0.2+0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1+ϵt.\begin{aligned} x_t&=0.5x_{t-1}+c\,y_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t},\\ y_t&=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

Current shocks have variance one and correlation rr. Shock pairs are independent across dates.

Case Feedback cc Shock correlation rr
Baseline 0 0
Shared current shocks 0 0.7
Lagged feedback only 0.2 0

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.4.] All cases have stable joint dynamics. In the shared-shock case epsilon is the structural DGP disturbance but not an innovation relative to the information set including current x. The purpose is to break that assumption deliberately. Do not call every disturbance an innovation relative to every possible information set.

Live code: the for-loop is the model

LIVE CODE · build, fit, then change one assumption 
# Excerpt from ardl_simulator(); initialization is in the full helper.
epsilon_x <- rnorm(total)
epsilon <- shock_corr * epsilon_x +
  sqrt(1 - shock_corr^2) * rnorm(total)
for (t in 2:total) {
  x[t] <- 0.5*x[t-1] + feedback*y[t-1] + epsilon_x[t]
  y[t] <- 0.2 + 0.6*y[t-1] + 0.4*x[t] +
    0.2*x[t-1] + epsilon[t]
}
Which change should move OLS away from the structural coefficient 0.4?

[7 minutes. Source: notes §8.4, canonical helpers/ardl_utils.R.] This is a visible excerpt from the canonical simulator, not a new function. Complete runnable live setup from the project root (or use the helper directly):

set.seed(637608)
n <- 400L; burn_in <- 200L; total <- n + burn_in + 1L
shock_corr <- 0; feedback <- 0
epsilon_x <- rnorm(total)
epsilon <- shock_corr * epsilon_x +
  sqrt(1 - shock_corr^2) * rnorm(total)
x <- y <- numeric(total)
for (t in 2:total) {
  x[t] <- 0.5*x[t-1] + feedback*y[t-1] + epsilon_x[t]
  y[t] <- 0.2 + 0.6*y[t-1] + 0.4*x[t] +
    0.2*x[t-1] + epsilon[t]
}
keep <- (burn_in + 2L):total
d <- data.frame(y=y[keep], x=x[keep])
d$y_lag1 <- c(NA, head(d$y, -1))
d$x_lag1 <- c(NA, head(d$x, -1))
coef(lm(y ~ y_lag1 + x + x_lag1, data=d))

Show the equation’s order: x_t is generated before y_t. Change shock_corr to .7, then instead set feedback=.2, shock_corr=0. Use the same underlying draws by resetting the seed for the three single samples. Larger n does not cure a wrong target.

One sample is not the distribution

More observations reduce sampling noise. They cannot identify the structural coefficient from an invalid restriction.

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.4; make_figures.R reproduces seed637609,200replications,n400.] Blue dashed line .4 is the structural coefficient; shared-shock estimates cluster near the conditional target1.1. Feedback-only estimates remain near .4 with finite sample variation. All cases keep the structural outcome equation unchanged. The simulation is serial, not a parallel benchmark. Ask what n=2000 would do.

The wrong structural answer can have clean residuals

What did the ACF check—and what did it leave unanswered?

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.4, shared-shock-residuals.] This is the seed637608 single sample. ACF measures residual serial dependence. Even population serial independence in the conditional residual would not establish that the estimated coefficients are the structural coefficients. Students should now revisit their Module5 jury metaphor: the jury answers the charge it hears.

OLS is answering a different conditional question

For the Gaussian shared-shock case,

E[ϵt∣ϵx,t]=0.7ϵx,t,ϵx,t=xt−0.5xt−1.E[\epsilon_t\mid\epsilon_{x,t}]=0.7\epsilon_{x,t}, \qquad \epsilon_{x,t}=x_t-0.5x_{t-1}.

Therefore,

E[yt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0.2+0.6yt−1+1.1xt−0.15xt−1.E[y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t] =0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+1.1x_t-0.15x_{t-1}.

Coefficient Structural DGP Conditional regression
Current xx 0.4 1.1
Lagged xx 0.2 −0.15
A useful conditional predictor need not recover the causal mechanism we wanted.

[5 minutes. Source: notes §8.4, Why the Shared-Shock Regression Can Still Look Clean.] Present the two coefficient adjustments aloud: .4+.7 and .2−.7*.5; the complete calculation below is available for student reference. The residual after projection is epsilon_t−.7epsilon_x,t, independent of current x innovations and serially independent in this construction. Thus clean residuals are entirely compatible with the observed coefficient pattern. Pause for a ten-minute break after this slide. Application bridge: claims may signal omitted labor news.

Student reference — the complete conditional-mean calculation. In this case there is no feedback (c=0c=0). Construct independent standard normal variables ϵx,t\epsilon_{x,t} and ηt\eta_t, independently across dates, and set

ϵt=0.7ϵx,t+1−0.72ηt=0.7ϵx,t+0.51ηt.\begin{aligned} \epsilon_t&=0.7\epsilon_{x,t}+\sqrt{1-0.7^2}\,\eta_t\\ &=0.7\epsilon_{x,t}+\sqrt{0.51}\,\eta_t. \end{aligned}

The structural disturbance has variance 0.72+0.51=10.7^2+0.51=1 and covariance 0.7 with the unit-variance predictor innovation. Their correlation is therefore 0.7. Independence and the zero mean of ηt\eta_t imply

E[ϵt∣ϵx,t]=0.7ϵx,t+0.51E[ηt∣ϵx,t]=0.7ϵx,t.\begin{aligned} E[\epsilon_t\mid\epsilon_{x,t}] &=0.7\epsilon_{x,t}+\sqrt{0.51}\,E[\eta_t\mid\epsilon_{x,t}]\\ &=0.7\epsilon_{x,t}. \end{aligned}

Since the predictor follows xt=0.5xt−1+ϵx,tx_t=0.5x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}, observing current xtx_t and its history reveals

ϵx,t=xt−0.5xt−1.\epsilon_{x,t}=x_t-0.5x_{t-1}.

The current ηt\eta_t remains independent of that information and of the past. Take the conditional expectation of the structural outcome equation and then substitute for the predictor innovation:

E[yt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0.2+0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1+E[ϵt∣ℱt−1,xt]=0.2+0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1+0.7(xt−0.5xt−1)=0.2+0.6yt−1+(0.4+0.7)xt+(0.2−0.7×0.5)xt−1=0.2+0.6yt−1+1.1xt−0.15xt−1.\begin{aligned} E[y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t] &=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+E[\epsilon_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\\ &=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+0.7(x_t-0.5x_{t-1})\\ &=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+(0.4+0.7)x_t\\ &\qquad+(0.2-0.7\times0.5)x_{t-1}\\ &=0.2+0.6y_{t-1}+1.1x_t-0.15x_{t-1}. \end{aligned}

Call the remaining population conditional disturbance ϵtc\epsilon_t^c:

ϵtc=yt−E[yt∣ℱt−1,xt]=ϵt−0.7ϵx,t=0.51ηt,Var(ϵtc)=0.51.\begin{aligned} \epsilon_t^c &=y_t-E[y_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1},x_t]\\ &=\epsilon_t-0.7\epsilon_{x,t}\\ &=\sqrt{0.51}\,\eta_t,\\ \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_t^c)&=0.51. \end{aligned}

It is independent of current ϵx,t\epsilon_{x,t} and of the past, and is iid across dates in this construction. It is not the original structural disturbance ϵt\epsilon_t, and it is not the finite-sample fitted residual ete_t. Estimated residuals approximate this conditional disturbance; estimation still induces finite-sample restrictions on them. Thus a residual ACF can look clean while OLS approaches 1.1 and −0.15-0.15 instead of the structural 0.4 and 0.2. The shared news has entered the conditional coefficients, not disappeared from the mechanism.

Act IV · Follow every path

A coefficient is one route. A response follows all routes.

One ARDL(1,1) example, reused. Conditional input experiments hold initial y history and outcome shocks fixed. Real-data transformation caution comes in ActV.

First specify the input experiment

yt=0.6yt−1+0.4xt+0.2xt−1+ϵty_t=0.6y_{t-1}+0.4x_t+0.2x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t

Imposed change in xx Today Next period Later
Pulse +1 0 0
Permanent step +1 +1 +1

Hold initial outcome history and outcome shocks fixed; compare the two yy paths.

Should a one-period pulse and a permanent step have the same long-run response?

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.5.] The intercept cancels between paths. Say conditional experiment: these are imposed x paths, not automatically paths generated by an innovation to x’s equation. Under stable dynamics our pulse decays, whereas the permanent step has a nonzero limit.

Student reference — subtracting two paths. Label the baseline path (0)(0) and the altered-input path (1)(1). Both satisfy the same ARDL with the same parameters and outcome shocks:

yt+h(a)=α+ϕ1yt+h−1(a)+β0xt+h(a)+β1xt+h−1(a)+ϵt+h,a∈{0,1}.\begin{aligned} y_{t+h}^{(a)}&=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t+h-1}^{(a)} +\beta_0x_{t+h}^{(a)}\\ &\qquad+\beta_1x_{t+h-1}^{(a)}+\epsilon_{t+h}, \qquad a\in\{0,1\}. \end{aligned}

Define cross-path deviations dy,h=yt+h(1)−yt+h(0)d_{y,h}=y_{t+h}^{(1)}-y_{t+h}^{(0)} and dx,h=xt+h(1)−xt+h(0)d_{x,h}=x_{t+h}^{(1)}-x_{t+h}^{(0)}. These compare two paths at the same date; they are not the time difference Δyt=yt−yt−1\Delta y_t=y_t-y_{t-1}. Subtracting yields

dy,h=(α−α)+ϕ1dy,h−1+β0dx,h+β1dx,h−1+(ϵt+h−ϵt+h)=ϕ1dy,h−1+β0dx,h+β1dx,h−1.\begin{aligned} d_{y,h}&=(\alpha-\alpha)+\phi_1d_{y,h-1} +\beta_0d_{x,h}\\ &\qquad+\beta_1d_{x,h-1}+(\epsilon_{t+h}-\epsilon_{t+h})\\ &=\phi_1d_{y,h-1}+\beta_0d_{x,h}+\beta_1d_{x,h-1}. \end{aligned}

Identical histories imply dy,h=dx,h=0d_{y,h}=d_{x,h}=0 before h=0h=0. For an imposed pulse, dx,0=1d_{x,0}=1 and dx,h=0d_{x,h}=0 for h≠0h\ne0. For a permanent step, dx,h=1d_{x,h}=1 for every h≥0h\ge0. The same recurrence handles both experiments; only the supplied predictor path changes. This is a conditional calculation holding the model and shocks fixed, not by itself an identified causal claim.

mh=ϕ1h−1(ϕ1β0+β1),h≥1.m_h=\phi_1^{h-1}(\phi_1\beta_0+\beta_1),\qquad h\ge1.

Pulse decays; repeated pulses accumulate

m2=0.264,step at h=2=0.4+0.44+0.264=1.104.m_2=0.264,\qquad \text{step at }h=2=0.4+0.44+0.264=1.104.

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.5.] The permanent step is a sequence of pulses; linear time-invariant dynamics make its response equal the cumulative pulse response. Say which experiment each curve depicts. One example only; notes keep the negative-phi cancellation case.

Student reference — why the step equals the cumulative pulse response. A unit step is a unit pulse at date tt, another at t+1t+1, and another at every later date. Linearity permits adding their responses; time-invariant coefficients make a pulse introduced at t+jt+j contribute mh−jm_{h-j} at t+ht+h. Denote the step response at horizon hh by shs_h. Then

sh=mh+mh−1+⋯+m0=∑j=0hmh−j=∑r=0hmr.\begin{aligned} s_h&=m_h+m_{h-1}+\cdots+m_0\\ &=\sum_{j=0}^{h}m_{h-j}=\sum_{r=0}^{h}m_r. \end{aligned}

s0=0.4,s1=0.4+0.44=0.84,s2=0.4+0.44+0.264=1.104,s3=1.104+0.1584=1.2624.\begin{aligned} s_0&=0.4,\\ s_1&=0.4+0.44=0.84,\\ s_2&=0.4+0.44+0.264=1.104,\\ s_3&=1.104+0.1584=1.2624. \end{aligned}

For example, s2=0.6(0.84)+0.6=1.104s_2=0.6(0.84)+0.6=1.104. This is accumulation of the full pulse responses, including outcome persistence, not just a sum of direct β\beta coefficients.

The long-run multiplier needs stability

Long-run step multiplier=∑ℓ=0qβℓ1−∑j=1pϕj\text{Long-run step multiplier} =\frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell}{1-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j}

0.4+0.21−0.6=1.5\frac{0.4+0.2}{1-0.6}=1.5

  • A permanent +1 in xx eventually changes yy by +1.5.
  • The one-period pulse itself converges to zero.
  • Estimated multipliers carry hats; a denominator near zero makes estimates sensitive.
If φ₁ = 1.05, does the nonzero denominator make −12 an eventual response?

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.5.] Use the path picture during presentation; the full algebra below supports student reference after class. This is a change, not the unconditional mean. Units must be y-units per x-unit. Joint coefficient uncertainty matters, but delta method stays in the Technical Note. The next slide answers the question by examining the path.

Student reference — the general steady-state difference. Let shs_h denote the response to a permanent unit increase in the imposed predictor path. For h≥qh\ge q, every included predictor lag is one unit above baseline:

sh=∑j=1pϕjsh−j+∑ℓ=0qβℓ.s_h=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_js_{h-j}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell.

Stability makes the transient responses vanish, so shs_h converges to a common limit s∞s_\infty. Taking that limit and collecting terms gives

s∞=(∑j=1pϕj)s∞+∑ℓ=0qβℓ,(1−∑j=1pϕj)s∞=∑ℓ=0qβℓ,s∞=∑ℓ=0qβℓ1−∑j=1pϕj.\begin{aligned} s_\infty&=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j\right)s_\infty +\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell,\\ \left(1-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j\right)s_\infty &=\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell,\\ s_\infty&=\frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell} {1-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j}. \end{aligned}

The intercept has already canceled between the two paths. For a predictor level x‾\bar x, the deterministic equilibrium level is instead y‾=[α+(∑ℓβℓ)x‾]/[1−∑jϕj]\bar y=[\alpha+(\sum_\ell\beta_\ell)\bar x]/[1-\sum_j\phi_j]. The multiplier describes a change between equilibria, not that level.

Student reference — summing our ARDL(1,1) responses. Since m0=β0m_0=\beta_0 and mh=ϕ1h−1(ϕ1β0+β1)m_h=\phi_1^{h-1}(\phi_1\beta_0+\beta_1) for h≥1h\ge1,

∑h=0∞mh=β0+(ϕ1β0+β1)∑k=0∞ϕ1k=β0+ϕ1β0+β11−ϕ1=β0+β11−ϕ1,|ϕ1|<1.\begin{aligned} \sum_{h=0}^{\infty}m_h &=\beta_0+(\phi_1\beta_0+\beta_1) \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\phi_1^k\\ &=\beta_0+\frac{\phi_1\beta_0+\beta_1}{1-\phi_1}\\ &=\frac{\beta_0+\beta_1}{1-\phi_1},\qquad |\phi_1|<1. \end{aligned}

Numerically, 0.4+0.44/(1−0.6)=0.4+1.1=1.50.4+0.44/(1-0.6)=0.4+1.1=1.5. Meanwhile mh=0.44(0.6)h−1→0m_h=0.44(0.6)^{h-1}\rightarrow0: the pulse fades even though the step converges to 1.5. For finite h≥1h\ge1, the step response is

sh=0.4+0.441−0.6h1−0.6=1.5−1.1(0.6)h.s_h=0.4+0.44\frac{1-0.6^h}{1-0.6}=1.5-1.1(0.6)^h.

Optional generalization from the notes’ Deeper Dive. Stability with finite predictor lags makes the pulse responses absolutely summable. Sum the general pulse recurrence and shift indices, using mh=0m_h=0 at negative horizons:

∑h=0∞mh=∑ℓ=0qβℓ+∑j=1pϕj∑h=0∞mh−j=∑ℓ=0qβℓ+(∑j=1pϕj)∑h=0∞mh.\begin{aligned} \sum_{h=0}^{\infty}m_h &=\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell +\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}m_{h-j}\\ &=\sum_{\ell=0}^{q}\beta_\ell +\left(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\phi_j\right) \sum_{h=0}^{\infty}m_h. \end{aligned}

Rearranging recovers the same ratio. Absolute summability justifies these infinite sums; a nonzero denominator alone does not justify taking a long-run limit.

Break it: a finite ratio can describe no limit

At φ₁ = 1.05 the path grows. The algebraic ratio −12 is not its limit.

In the independent-shock, no-feedback baseline,

xt=0.5xt−1+ϵx,t.x_t=0.5x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}.

What else must be followed if x responds to past y?

[4 minutes. Source: notes §8.5.] Hold the outcome shock path fixed for this comparison. Shared current shocks could also change the expected outcome disturbance; .64 is the mechanical input path contribution only outside the independent-shock baseline. With feedback, follow both equations. That motivates the later VAR—not an automatic causal solution. Application bridge: a step in claims growth is not a step in the level of claims.

Student reference — trace the predictor innovation before the outcome. In the independent-shock, no-feedback baseline, compare paths with identical initial histories and shocks except for a one-unit increase in ϵx,t\epsilon_{x,t}. Keep every outcome innovation fixed. dx,0=1,dx,h=0.5dx,h−1=(0.5)h.d_{x,0}=1,\qquad d_{x,h}=0.5d_{x,h-1}=(0.5)^h.

Act V · A predictor needs a calendar

Initial claims and unemployment, with an honest forecast origin.

One real-data application pays off the simulation: inspect transformations, justify timing, select a modest lag menu on a common sample, diagnose, revise once using training data, and evaluate the intended use. No causal multiplier is estimated for the observational claims example.

The familiar workflow gets two new questions

Inspect → specifyUnits, transformations, lag lengths, release dates.
Estimate → diagnoseCommon estimation sample; residual plots and regression diagnostics.
Revise → evaluateTraining-only choices; identical holdout dates and benchmarks.
When was x available?
What interpretation do the assumptions support?

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.6.] Common sample matters because different maximum lags otherwise discard different initial rows. IC conventions unchanged from M4; lm likelihood counts variance. ACF/PACF of y alone cannot select all cross-variable lags. Neither low BIC nor a clean residual plot establishes exogeneity.

A future outcome may need a future predictor

ỹt+1∣t=α̂+ϕ̂1yt+β̂0x̃t+1∣t+β̂1xt\tilde y_{t+1\mid t}=\hat\alpha+\hat\phi_1y_t +\hat\beta_0\tilde x_{t+1\mid t}+\hat\beta_1x_t

Information about future xx Claim we can make
Forecast from its own model Forecast with predictor uncertainty
Stipulated path Conditional / scenario forecast
Released before the target outcome Nowcast using that information
If an evaluation substitutes the future realized x, what advantage has it given the model?

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.6.] The notes’ feasible-versus-oracle simulation is the optional live extension if students need to see leakage. No new chart needed. The error can include beta0 times x forecast error plus the outcome innovation; predictor uncertainty and any covariance matter. A scenario band intentionally conditions on x. Lag-only models avoid future x at one step only when lagged data are released.

Student reference — derive the one-step forecast. Start with the true ARDL(1,1) at the target date:

yt+1=α+ϕ1yt+β0xt+1+β1xt+ϵt+1.y_{t+1}=\alpha+\phi_1y_t+\beta_0x_{t+1}+\beta_1x_t+\epsilon_{t+1}.

Assume yt,xty_t,x_t are available in ℱt\mathcal F_t, and the sequential restriction holds at t+1t+1. By iterated expectations,

E[ϵt+1∣ℱt]=E[E[ϵt+1∣ℱt,xt+1]∣ℱt]=0.\begin{aligned} E[\epsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t] &=E\!\left[E[\epsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t,x_{t+1}] \mid\mathcal F_t\right]=0. \end{aligned}

Taking the conditional expectation of the target equation gives

E[yt+1∣ℱt]=α+ϕ1yt+β1xt+β0E[xt+1∣ℱt].\begin{aligned} E[y_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t] &=\alpha+\phi_1y_t+\beta_1x_t\\ &\qquad+\beta_0E[x_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]. \end{aligned}

Replace the unknown coefficients by estimates and the predictor conditional mean by its feasible forecast to obtain the slide’s plug-in expression. If xtx_t or yty_t has not yet been released, it cannot simply be inserted as known; the information set and forecasting problem must change accordingly.

Student reference — separate predictor uncertainty from outcome noise. First hold parameters known and use the true predictor conditional mean. Define vt+1=xt+1−E[xt+1∣ℱt]v_{t+1}=x_{t+1}-E[x_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]. Subtraction gives

yt+1−E[yt+1∣ℱt]=β0vt+1+ϵt+1.\begin{aligned} y_{t+1}-E[y_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t] &=\beta_0v_{t+1}+\epsilon_{t+1}. \end{aligned}

In general, the variance of this sum includes 2β0Cov(vt+1,ϵt+1∣ℱt)2\beta_0\operatorname{Cov}(v_{t+1},\epsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t). Under the maintained sequential conditional-mean restriction that covariance is zero, because vt+1v_{t+1} is known given ℱt,xt+1\mathcal F_t,x_{t+1} and E[vt+1ϵt+1∣ℱt]=0E[v_{t+1}\epsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]=0 by iterated expectations. Thus in this maintained known-parameter case,

Var(yt+1∣ℱt)=β02Var(xt+1∣ℱt)+Var(ϵt+1∣ℱt).\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(y_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t) &=\beta_0^2\operatorname{Var}(x_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t)\\ &\qquad+\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t). \end{aligned}

This formula does not include parameter-estimation uncertainty. A conditional scenario calculation with a fixed predictor path intentionally removes the predictor uncertainty; it answers a different question.

Student reference — feasible versus oracle with the same fitted coefficients. Let the oracle insert realized xt+1x_{t+1} while the feasible forecast inserts x̃t+1∣t\tilde x_{t+1\mid t}. Their difference is exactly

ỹt+1∣toracle−ỹt+1∣tfeasible=β̂0(xt+1−x̃t+1∣t).\begin{aligned} \tilde y_{t+1\mid t}^{\mathrm{oracle}} -\tilde y_{t+1\mid t}^{\mathrm{feasible}} &=\hat\beta_0(x_{t+1}-\tilde x_{t+1\mid t}). \end{aligned}

Since forecast error is actual minus forecast,

et+1∣tfeasible=et+1∣toracle+β̂0(xt+1−x̃t+1∣t),et+1∣toracle=ϵt+1+(α−α̂)+(ϕ1−ϕ̂1)yt+(β0−β̂0)xt+1+(β1−β̂1)xt.\begin{aligned} e_{t+1\mid t}^{\mathrm{feasible}} &=e_{t+1\mid t}^{\mathrm{oracle}} +\hat\beta_0(x_{t+1}-\tilde x_{t+1\mid t}),\\ e_{t+1\mid t}^{\mathrm{oracle}} &=\epsilon_{t+1}+(\alpha-\hat\alpha) +(\phi_1-\hat\phi_1)y_t\\ &\qquad+(\beta_0-\hat\beta_0)x_{t+1} +(\beta_1-\hat\beta_1)x_t. \end{aligned}

The first identity is exact even with estimated coefficients. The second shows why an oracle error is not just the structural innovation when coefficients are estimated. Observing future xx removes one information gap; it does not remove estimation error or establish structural exogeneity. The resulting score is a feasible nowcast score only if that predictor was actually released at the forecast origin.

Reference month is not release date

One step ahead in the monthly index; usually a nowcast of the current calendar month.
Schematic timing, not an exact historical release calendar. Use ℐtrelease\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}} for this origin.

[4 minutes. Source: notes §§8.6–8.7.] Do not call this an end-of-prior-month forecast. The issue date must be after both releases; exact days can differ and can be delayed. We deliberately ignore partial target-month claims. Revised caches cannot recreate real-time vintages. The labels separate month end, arrival of both releases, and the issue date.

What are we actually modeling?

yt=ΔUt,xt=100ΔlogCty_t=\Delta U_t,\qquad x_t=100\Delta\log C_t

U: unemployment rateMonthly percent. y is its change in percentage points.
C: initial claimsMean of weekly counts whose week-ending Saturdays fall in the month.
x: claims growth100 × log change, approximately percent growth in that monthly mean.
A monthly mean of weekly claims is not a monthly total.

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.7; FRED UNRATE and ICSA cached under data/.] Both source series seasonally adjusted. Household-survey unemployment and administrative benefit claims cover different populations. A permanent step in x here means faster claims growth forever—not one additional claimant. Data checks reject missing weeks or months before aggregation and lag construction.

Student reference — transformations and units. If ntn_t weekly observations have week-ending Saturdays in reference month tt, the monthly predictor level is

Ct=1nt∑win month tICSAw.C_t=\frac{1}{n_t}\sum_{w\,\text{in month }t}\mathrm{ICSA}_w.

It remains a mean weekly claims count. It is not the sum of all claims during a calendar month. The modeled predictor is

xt=100(logCt−logCt−1)=100log(Ct/Ct−1),100(CtCt−1−1)=100[exp(xt/100)−1]≈xt.\begin{aligned} x_t&=100(\log C_t-\log C_{t-1})\\ &=100\log(C_t/C_{t-1}),\\ 100\left(\frac{C_t}{C_{t-1}}-1\right) &=100\big[\exp(x_t/100)-1\big]\approx x_t. \end{aligned}

The approximation uses exp(a)≈1+a\exp(a)\approx1+a for a small log change. Meanwhile yt=Ut−Ut−1y_t=U_t-U_{t-1} is a difference of rates recorded in percent, so its unit is percentage points, not percent growth.

To interpret a permanent one-unit increase in xx, compare paths with the same initial Ct−1C_{t-1} and add one to claims log growth at each date from tt onward. Summing those log-growth differences through horizon hh gives

logCt+h(1)−logCt+h(0)=(h+1)/100,Ct+h(1)Ct+h(0)=exp((h+1)/100).\begin{aligned} \log C_{t+h}^{(1)}-\log C_{t+h}^{(0)}&=(h+1)/100,\\ \frac{C_{t+h}^{(1)}}{C_{t+h}^{(0)}}&=\exp((h+1)/100). \end{aligned}

Thus a step in growth makes the claims-level ratio keep rising. A one-period pulse in growth would instead leave a constant level ratio exp(1/100)\exp(1/100) from that date onward. These are translations of the imposed input experiment, not causal estimates from the observational application.

Roll the information, keep the coefficients fixed

Observed lags update after release. Coefficients remain estimated on 1990–2017. No-change predicts ΔU = 0.

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.7 app-forecast and app-holdout-plot.] The plot shows changes rather than reconstructed levels for slide clarity; errors are identical because each level forecast adds observed U(t−1). These are24rolling one-step-index predictions, not a single24-step path fromDecember2017. The origin is the post-release information set, and all caches are revised historical data.

Student reference — reconstruct levels without changing one-step errors. At each post-release origin for target month tt, let ỹt∣ℐtrelease\tilde y_{t\mid \mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}} denote the predicted change using only available lags. The level prediction adds that change to the latest observed level:

Ũt∣ℐtrelease=Ut−1+ỹt∣ℐtrelease.\tilde U_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}} =U_{t-1}+\tilde y_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}}.

Since Ut=Ut−1+ytU_t=U_{t-1}+y_t, subtracting gives

Ut−Ũt∣ℐtrelease=(Ut−1+yt)−(Ut−1+ỹt∣ℐtrelease)=yt−ỹt∣ℐtrelease.\begin{aligned} U_t-\tilde U_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}} &=(U_{t-1}+y_t) -(U_{t-1}+\tilde y_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}})\\ &=y_t-\tilde y_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}}. \end{aligned}

The level and change errors are identical date by date, hence have identical RMSE and MAE. A no-change level forecast sets Ũt∣ℐtrelease=Ut−1\tilde U_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}}=U_{t-1}, equivalently ỹt∣ℐtrelease=0\tilde y_{t\mid\mathcal I_t^{\mathrm{release}}}=0. At the next origin the newly released UtU_t becomes the observed lag. Accumulating all predicted changes from December 2017 would replace those observed lags with a different recursive forecasting experiment.

[3 minutes. Source: notes §8.7 app-scores, exact values verified by make_figures.R.] No significance claim or DM test;24dates is a narrow window. Retuning on these errors would consume the holdout. No causal intervention interpretation. The complete application deliberately shows imperfect diagnostics rather than manufacturing an all-green result. That is the practical exogeneity lesson.

Student reference — scores and their units. For each model MM and each of the same 24 holdout dates, let eM,te_{M,t} be observed minus predicted unemployment change. The preceding slide shows that it is also the corresponding level error. Compute

MSEM=124∑tin holdouteM,t2,RMSEM=MSEM,MAEM=124∑tin holdout|eM,t|.\begin{aligned} \mathrm{MSE}_M&=\frac{1}{24}\sum_{t\,\text{in holdout}}e_{M,t}^2,\\ \mathrm{RMSE}_M&=\sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}_M},\\ \mathrm{MAE}_M&=\frac{1}{24}\sum_{t\,\text{in holdout}}|e_{M,t}|. \end{aligned}

The errors are percentage points, MSE is squared percentage points, and taking the square root returns RMSE to percentage points. The application code applies these formulas to the fixed-coefficient predictions: ARDL RMSE rounds to 0.1057 and MAE to 0.0831. For no change, the errors are simply the realized ΔUt\Delta U_t, giving RMSE 0.1099 and MAE 0.0875 after rounding. No denominator or evaluation date changes between models. The inequalities in this table describe this window; the arithmetic itself supplies neither a significance test nor a causal claim.

Act VI · Three doors out of ARDL

Brief orientation to the next modules.

The following three topic slides are Looking Ahead, optional orientation only. They do not expand Module8’s assessable Core. No testing code or new complete four-step workflow: Modules9–12 develop those methods properly.

Looking Ahead: does x’s past add predictive information?

MODULE 9 · GRANGER CAUSALITY · OPTIONAL PREVIEW

For a lag-only linear model and a stated conditioning set,

H0:β1=β2=⋯=βq=0.H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2=\cdots=\beta_q=0.

A joint question: do these xx lags add information beyond the history already included?

Predictive precedence can arise from an early signal of a common driver. It does not identify an intervention effect.
Would adding another predictor potentially change this answer?

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.8, LookingAhead.] Yes—the information set matters. Including current x and testing its lags asks a different question. Do not teach the F reference distribution or testing workflow here. One insignificant coefficient is not a joint test. Name both directions as a possibility; Module9 develops it.

Looking Ahead: can wandering levels share a stable gap?

MODULE 10 · COINTEGRATION · OPTIONAL PREVIEW

yt∼I(1),xt∼I(1),yt−a−bxt∼I(0).y_t\sim I(1),\qquad x_t\sim I(1),\qquad y_t-a-bx_t\sim I(0).

Harry and his dog, Mouse: both wander, but their separation can remain stationary.

  • Cointegration concerns a stationary combination of nonstationary levels.
  • An error-correction model links short-run changes to last period’s deviation.
  • Rewriting an ARDL as an ECM is algebra, not a cointegration test.
What would differ if they wandered independently with no stable separation?

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.9, LookingAhead.] Keep the existing Harry-and-Mouse leash analogy for Module10; no large cartoon sequence or new simulation here. Ordinary ADF critical values do not automatically apply to estimated cointegrating residuals. Bounds testing/Johansen stay outside this introduction. Alpha remains the intercept; the optional reference below writes the adjustment coefficient explicitly as phi1−1.

Optional preview reference — the full error-correction rearrangement. This is the algebra in notes §8.9, not additional Module 8 assessable content. Start with the level ARDL(1,1):

yt=α+ϕ1yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵt.y_t=\alpha+\phi_1y_{t-1}+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t.

Subtract yt−1y_{t-1} from both sides:

Δyt=α+(ϕ1−1)yt−1+β0xt+β1xt−1+ϵt.\begin{aligned} \Delta y_t&=\alpha+(\phi_1-1)y_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+\beta_0x_t+\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

Substitute xt=xt−1+Δxtx_t=x_{t-1}+\Delta x_t and collect the two lagged-level terms:

Δyt=α+(ϕ1−1)yt−1+β0(xt−1+Δxt)+β1xt−1+ϵt=α+(ϕ1−1)yt−1+(β0+β1)xt−1+β0Δxt+ϵt.\begin{aligned} \Delta y_t&=\alpha+(\phi_1-1)y_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+\beta_0(x_{t-1}+\Delta x_t) +\beta_1x_{t-1}+\epsilon_t\\ &=\alpha+(\phi_1-1)y_{t-1}\\ &\qquad+(\beta_0+\beta_1)x_{t-1} +\beta_0\Delta x_t+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

When ϕ1≠1\phi_1\ne1, define the level-relation coefficients

a=α1−ϕ1,b=β0+β11−ϕ1.a=\frac{\alpha}{1-\phi_1},\qquad b=\frac{\beta_0+\beta_1}{1-\phi_1}.

Then the first three terms factor as

α+(ϕ1−1)yt−1+(β0+β1)xt−1=−(1−ϕ1)[yt−1−a−bxt−1].\begin{aligned} &\alpha+(\phi_1-1)y_{t-1} +(\beta_0+\beta_1)x_{t-1}\\ &\quad=-(1-\phi_1)[y_{t-1}-a-bx_{t-1}]. \end{aligned}

To check the signs, expand the bracket: the three terms are −(1−ϕ1)yt−1-(1-\phi_1)y_{t-1}, +(1−ϕ1)a=α+(1-\phi_1)a=\alpha, and +(1−ϕ1)bxt−1=(β0+β1)xt−1+(1-\phi_1)b x_{t-1}=(\beta_0+\beta_1)x_{t-1}. Therefore

Δyt=−(1−ϕ1)[yt−1−a−bxt−1]+β0Δxt+ϵt.\begin{aligned} \Delta y_t&=-(1-\phi_1)[y_{t-1}-a-bx_{t-1}]\\ &\qquad+\beta_0\Delta x_t+\epsilon_t. \end{aligned}

The bracket is the preceding period’s deviation from the level relation. When ϕ1<1\phi_1<1, a positive deviation contributes negatively to the next change, other inputs held fixed; this sign alone is not a full stability condition. The adjustment coefficient is ϕ1−1\phi_1-1, while α\alpha remains the original intercept. The coefficient bb reproduces the familiar long-run ratio.

This rewriting also works for stationary variables and therefore cannot prove cointegration. For I(1)I(1) variables, one must additionally establish that the level combination is I(0)I(0) and justify the conditioning and adjustment model. At ϕ1=1\phi_1=1 the unfactored difference equation is still valid, but division by 1−ϕ11-\phi_1 is unavailable. Module 10 supplies the statistical arguments and appropriate cointegration tests; no test is supplied by this algebra.

Looking Ahead: give every variable an equation

MODULES 11–12 · VAR AND SHOCK INTERPRETATION

yt=ay+byyyt−1+byxxt−1+ϵy,t,xt=ax+bxyyt−1+bxxxt−1+ϵx,t.\begin{aligned} y_t&=a_y+b_{yy}y_{t-1}+b_{yx}x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{y,t},\\ x_t&=a_x+b_{xy}y_{t-1}+b_{xx}x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{x,t}. \end{aligned}

The ensemble cast: both histories can help explain both outcomes.

A system models joint evolution and forecast feedback. It still needs assumptions to identify causal shocks.

[2 minutes. Source: notes §8.10, LookingAhead.] No claim that VAR is universally superior or structurally identified by default. Current reduced-form innovations may be correlated. The a/b subscripts distinguish the equations just as in the notes. The same cross-date arrows now belong to two equations, rather than treating x’s path as supplied to a single equation.

Key takeaways + next time

ARDL adds observed predictor history to outcome memory.

Exogeneity concerns the disturbance and the whole information set.

A response follows every path; state the input experiment first.

A forecast needs an honest calendar and a common benchmark.

Which interpretation do our assumptions justify? These are the three questions students should carry into multivariate modeling.
